paras: The threatened lynching of Kid Henderson occurred at Chandler, Oklahoma, in early August 1915, when Henderson, a Black man accused of a killing at nearby Wellston, was rushed to the state penitentiary to keep him from a lynching. Henderson pleaded guilty and was sentenced to prison, and no mob attack was reported.

According to a Chandler dispatch of August 4, Henderson had "murdered a farmer at Wellston last week" and was captured in the northwestern part of the state on Saturday, July 31. A later report from Newkirk instead named the dead man as Constable Henry Grinstaff of Wellston.

After his capture Henderson was brought back to Chandler, where he pleaded guilty, was sentenced to life imprisonment and was taken to the penitentiary at McAlester the day before the dispatch. The dispatch said his case "was handled quietly" and that he was hurried off "to avoid threatened lynching." It did not say who had made the threat or whether any crowd gathered.

On August 13 a Newkirk dispatch reported that the judge of the Lincoln County district court had that day sentenced Henderson to ninety-nine years for the killing of Grinstaff. No report of any arrest or prosecution of those who threatened the lynching appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers through a short item that The Oklahoma City Times ran on August 5 under the headline "MURDERER TO PEN," with the deck "Slayer of Wellston Farmer Hurried Off to Avoid Threatened Lynching." The Daily Ardmoreite printed the same text the next day. Both treated Henderson's guilt as settled, called him "the negro," and presented the threat only as the reason for moving him quickly.
The Topeka State Journal's later item, "Life Term for Oklahoma Slayer," gave only the sentence and did not mention the threat or Henderson's race. No Black-press coverage of the case was found.

The two dispatches disagree on the victim, calling him a farmer in the Chandler report and Constable Henry Grinstaff in the Newkirk report. They also differ on the sentence, life imprisonment by about August 3 against ninety-nine years on August 13, and the coverage does not explain whether the later item reports a separate hearing or a garbled account.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Kid Henderson
bases: A Black prisoner accused of murder was rushed to the state penitentiary after his sentencing 'to avoid threatened lynching' (A1); no mob action is reported, so this is a threatened lynching.
Henderson was not killed; he was sentenced in court and taken to McAlester (A1, A3), and the only violence reported is an unspecified 'threatened lynching' over the murder charge (A1).

The lynching threat appears only in one Chandler dispatch (A1, reprinted as A2); the separate Topeka item (A3) confirms that Henderson was prosecuted in Lincoln County for a Wellston killing but disagrees on the victim and sentence and does not mention a threat.

accounts.label: Chandler dispatch
accounts.gist: Henderson, who 'murdered a farmer at Wellston', was captured, pleaded guilty, got life and was hurried off to McAlester to avoid a threatened lynching.

accounts.label: Newkirk dispatch
accounts.gist: On Aug. 13 the Lincoln County district judge sentenced Henderson to ninety-nine years for killing Constable Henry Grinstaff of Wellston; no threat is mentioned.

framing.detail: Headlined 'MURDERER TO PEN' and 'Slayer of Wellston Farmer Hurried Off to Avoid Threatened Lynching', treating guilt as settled and the threat as a reason for haste.
The Daily Ardmoreite ran the same dispatch unchanged.
The Topeka State Journal headlined 'Life Term for Oklahoma Slayer' and gave only the sentence.

conflicts.note: The two dispatches do not agree on who was killed; neither is local, and the Topeka item gives a name.
